problem: VLM-based object navigation feeds VLMs only local, unstructured observations and queries them at every step to choose among frontier viewpoints. Because VLMs have weak 3D spatial understanding, this leads to backtracking, redundant exploration and high token cost.
motivation: Efficient zero-shot object navigation in large continuous multi-room environments needs a coherent global representation and a decision on when and how to query the VLM. The authors observe that room-level reasoning fits VLM strengths (semantics, layout), while low-level exploration is handled better by classic frontier methods.
key_idea: Build an incremental three-layer graph (viewpoint, object and room nodes) and use a two-stage policy: the VLM plans at room level, and frontier-based in-room exploration uses VLM-assisted early stop and VLM-based target verification.
insight: Moving VLM decisions from viewpoint level to room level improves results and cuts tokens: on HM3D, SR goes from 75.0 to 79.6, SPL from 34.9 to 38.7, and tokens per episode from 22935 to 8068. The representation ablation shows that object and room nodes are complementary (SR 71.3 with viewpoints only, 75.0 with all three layers). VLM verification matters most for SR (SR 72.1 without it versus 79.6).
method: Viewpoint nodes: skeleton graph built incrementally. Frontiers outside the current node's coverage are clustered into segments, a visibility graph is built over them, and maximum cliques are iteratively removed with each clique center becoming a viewpoint. Frontier-free regions contribute their center. Edges are straight-line traversability.

Object nodes: open-vocabulary detection (MM-GroundingDINO) and SAM masks are lifted to 3D with depth and pose. Nodes store position, point cloud, label, confidence and 3D box, and are merged across views. Objects are linked to viewpoints within the cover range.

Room nodes: walls are extracted from a top-down point-cloud histogram, the background is dilated iteratively to split connected components, and a watershed produces rooms. Rooms are linked to their viewpoints.

In-room exploration with early stop: frontiers are split into true frontiers (room boundaries) and inner frontiers (occlusions). The agent visits the nearest viewpoint with true frontiers until they are cleared. If only inner frontiers remain, the VLM decides whether to keep exploring the room.

Next Best Room: the prompt contains the target, current state, history and JSON of R (rooms-viewpoints-objects). The VLM uses chain-of-thought over semantic similarity and distance to pick a partially explored room. A penalized distance grows with steps taken and explored viewpoints, so the agent favors moving forward late in an episode.

VLM-based target verification: context-aware check of the detected object with its surroundings, such as rejecting a painting of a plant. Then a single re-verification from an optimal viewpoint sampled along the path (over 95% of the object visible, larger 2D box, size checks).
Low-level execution: forward 0.25 m and turn 30° with a 500-step budget, and Gemini-2.0-flash as the VLM.

setting.observation: posed RGB-D (640x480, HFOV 79°, depth 0.5-5 m); real robot uses a 360° RGB camera and LiDAR converted to depth
setting.action_space: low-level move_forward 0.25 m / turn_left / turn_right 30° / stop
setting.privileged: none (pose given as in the standard task)

numbers.eval_set_note: HM3D-v1, only episodes where the start and the target are on the same floor

numbers.evidence: Table 1 HM3D-v2 columns; Table 3 for SoftSPL and DTG

numbers_note: The paper does not specify official split names, so 'val' is used. The HM3D-v2 ablation tables are labelled 'HM3D'. The real-world results (average SR 81% over 100 episodes on 5 categories) are not simulated benchmarks and are omitted.
results: STRIVE beats 12 zero-shot and other baselines on all four benchmarks. Gains over the second best are +6.4 SR / +3.6 SPL on HM3D-v1, +13.1 / +6.2 on HM3D-v2 (79.6 vs DORAEMON's 66.5), +20.6 / +12.3 on RoboTHOR, and +11.2 / +5.5 on MP3D. On a real robot it achieves 81% average SR over 100 episodes on 5 categories (120 episodes in total across 10 environments).
limitations: Designed for single-floor navigation, so multi-floor HM3D-v1 episodes reduce performance (62.9 vs 72.7 on same-floor episodes).
Depends on Gemini API calls and on room segmentation and detection quality; real-world runtimes are around 63 s per episode.
Benchmark annotation errors (missing targets in HM3D and MP3D) cause false failures.
